expected_evidence: geological: elevated iridium/platinum-group-element anomaly layer coincident with ~10,950 BCE (Younger Dryas Boundary) in North American sediment/loess/lake cores
geological: magnetic spherules, nanodiamonds, meltglass, and shocked/melted quartz grains in the same stratigraphic horizon at multiple independent sites
geological: a 'black mat' or carbon-rich layer marking abrupt ecological disruption directly above the anomaly
astronomical: identification of a plausible impact crater, airburst structure, or cosmic-material signature (e.g., Fe-Ni spherules with extraterrestrial isotopic ratios) dated to the same interval
material/archaeological: disruption or abandonment horizon at Clovis-age sites, changes in lithic technology, or widespread biomass-burning/charcoal peaks synchronous with the anomaly
genetic: ancient-DNA signatures of a sudden population bottleneck in North American megafauna (mammoth, horse, etc.) time-correlated with the layer

model_prior: the existing (contested) scientific literature on the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (Firestone et al. 2007 and successors) reporting exactly these proxies, alongside published critiques disputing reproducibility
oral_tradition: speculative correlations drawn by some proponents to Native American oral narratives of fire/flood cataclysms (low reliability, hard to date precisely)
response.rationale: The hypothesis pins a very specific date (~10,950 BCE) that coincides almost exactly with the Younger Dryas onset boundary, so I treat the relevant period as 'younger-dryas' rather than the broader 'upper-paleolithic' bucket, since that is when the diagnostic geochemical signature would be deposited. For this period, geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7) channels are the most detectability-favorable — sediment/ice/lake-core stratigraphy from ~13,000 years ago is routinely preserved and sampled, and extraterrestrial-material proxies (Ir/Pt anomalies, spherules, nanodiamonds) are exactly the kind of thing geoarchaeology is built to find. Material/archaeological evidence (0.35) and genetic evidence (0.3) are much weaker channels this far back — organic preservation, faunal DNA, and site-level correlation are patchy. Oral tradition (0.1), linguistic (0.05), iconographic (0.1), and textual (0.0) are effectively non-informative at this time depth. Because this is a real, actively studied hypothesis (the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis), evidence of the proposed type has in fact been reported at multiple North American sites (model-prior, unverified against the evidence text given to me), though it remains scientifically contested — some independent labs failed to replicate the anomalies, and no confirmed impact crater has been identified. This mixed empirical record is consistent with moderate-to-good detectability rather than a total absence of evidence, so a low-detectability explanation for silence is not strongly needed here — there IS evidence, it's just disputed rather than absent. I set my own adjustment (0.5) slightly below the raw geological/astronomical scores to reflect that: (a) 13,000 years introduces real taphonomic loss/bioturbation risk even in favorable geological contexts, and (b) the archaeological/genetic corroboration channels that would strengthen a 'triggered by cosmic impact' causal claim (as opposed to a mere coincident anomaly) are considerably weaker, pulling down the composite detectability for the full causal chain implied by the hypothesis.
